title: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Simple rules with complex behavior, such as the rule 30 cellular automaton sampled sparsely to give an encrypting sequence, can be used to build stream ciphers at least as secure against cryptanalysis as any known system, unlike additive cellular automata or linear feedback shift registers, whose keys are easily recovered.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I strongly suspect that they can, and that in fact they allow one to construct systems that are at least as secure to cryptanalysis as any that are known.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Cryptography and Cryptanalysis” (from p. 598), p. 603. Scope: stream ciphers based on cellular automata, specifically rule 30

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Concrete rule-30 constructions can be cryptanalyzed now and may be decisively refuted. The comparative superlative and lack of a precise construction prevent confirmation of the claim as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix the rule-30 cipher construction, key schedule, sampling pattern, and security notion, then subject it to public cryptanalytic attacks and reductions against standardized stream ciphers. A practical key-recovery or distinguishing attack refutes the construction; failure of known attacks does not establish maximal security.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Absence of a known attack is not proof of security.

The cipher and security parameter are underspecified.

As secure as any known system has no fixed benchmark.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.48
data existence: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The cipher construction is explicit enough that published attack costs can be compared with those of standardized stream ciphers, using only public descriptions and generated keystream. That can refute a claim of matching the best known systems if a cheaper break exists for the stated variant. It cannot prove comparable security, because an undiscovered attack remains possible and the comparison class keeps growing.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix the sparsely sampled rule-30 keystream construction and compare the cost of the best published cryptanalysis with the published attack costs of standard stream ciphers. A cheaper complete break refutes 'at least as secure as any known system'; the absence of a break does not establish that equivalence.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Any known system' is an open-ended comparison class.

Sparse sampling changes the attack surface relative to earlier rule-30 proposals, so a break of one variant is not automatically a break of the other.
